title: Ingress pricing & QoS simulation notebook
body:
Purpose:
Quick experimental notebook for simulating how ingress pricing signals + per-tenant QoS budgets affect routing, burst reservations, and latency SLOs. This is a personal scratchpad — messy math, ideas, and TODOs. Goal is to get a simple sim we can later turn into a small harness (python/ts) and a short experiment doc for PM/infra to review.

High-level idea:
- Each tenant issues requests that have a value (business importance) and latency sensitivity (p50 target).
- Router picks a route for each request: hosted / dedicated / fallback variant. Each route has a cost-per-token (or cost-per-request) and capacity (rps) and an observed latency distribution function.
- Tenants have a daily QoS budget (tokens or $) and a soft price-sensitivity parameter alpha that determines how aggressively they accept cheaper but slower routes.
- Ingress pricing signal: dynamic per-route price that increases when utilization > threshold. Router can use price + latency score to pick route.

Simplified sim model (first pass):
- Time discrete, 1s steps, sim horizon 1h (3600 steps).
- Tenants: N = 50 (mix of small/med/large). Each tenant generates requests per second sampled from Poisson(lambda).
- Request attributes: expected token_count ~ Poisson(40), priority_score in {low, med, high} mapped to values {0.5, 1, 2}.
- Routes: hosted (cheap, latency mean=120ms, p95=250ms, baseline cost=0.6 units/token), dedicated (expensive, latency mean=40ms, p95=90ms, cost=1.2 units/token), fallback (ultra-cheap quantized variant, latency mean=300ms, cost=0.25 un/token). Capacity slots: hosted cap 200 rps, dedicated pooled cap scaled by tenant weight.
- Price function: price(route) = base_cost * (1 + beta * max(0, util - util_thresh)), util = current_rps/route_cap. beta tunable (0..3). util_thresh default 0.7.
- Tenant route choice: choose route r that minimizes: effective_cost = price(r) * token_count / value_multiplier + gamma * latency_penalty(latency_p95 - target_p95)/target_p95, where gamma trades off cost vs latency. If tenant QoS budget exhausted, force cheapest route.

Initial parameter hypotheses to test:
- beta low (0.3) -> prices barely change, congestion causes latency spikes on hosted, dedicated underutilized.
- beta high (2.0) -> quick price surge, traffic migrates earlier to dedicated or fallback, overall p95 improves but cost rises for high-value tenants.
- gamma low (0.1) -> tenants cost-seeking; gamma high (5.0) -> latency-sensitive tenants crowd dedicated.
- util_thresh 0.7 vs 0.9.

Metrics to capture per-sim run:
- global p50/p95/p99 latency per route and weighted across tenants
- cost per tenant and aggregate daily spend (sim scaled to 1d)
- fraction of requests hitting fallback variant
- number of QoS budget breaches (requests forced to cheaper route)
- tail amplification events (periods where many tenants see p95 blowups simultaneously)

Rough toy numbers (manual calcs/intuition):
- If hosted cap fills to 250 rps vs 200 rps, p95 may jump from 250ms -> 600ms (nonlinear), causing p95-weighted penalty to spike.
- With beta=2: price hosted goes from 0.6 -> ~1.2 when util hits 0.8, which makes dedicated price competitive for medium-high token_count requests.

Open questions / things to represent more faithfully later:
- Request composition: some requests are short ctrl-signal (few tokens) but have highest latency sensitivity (API calls). Need multi-class request modeling.
- KV cache or prefix cache effects: some requests hit cache and are cheap/fast; price signals should consider effective token count.
- Burst reservations: modeling per-tenant burst buckets (credit) and how they deplete/replenish across time windows.
- Server-side backpressure: how router behaves when route returns 429 or degraded errors. Do we auto-fallback or queue?
- Cold-start / warmup costs for quantized fallback variants (higher error rate) — include quality penalty function.

Experimental plan (next steps):
1) Build minimal sim (python, pandas) implementing model above with pluggable parameters. Keep runs parameterized (seedable). Target: prototype in ~2 days.
2) Add multi-class requests + burst bucket model. Add simple cache hit probability per tenant. (2 days)
3) Run grid of (beta, gamma, util_thresh) with N=50 tenants and 3 route configs. Collect metrics and plot heatmaps: cost vs p95 vs fallback fraction. (2 days)
4) Draft a 1-pager for PM/infra with top-3 tradeoffs and recommended defaults for price-signal beta and util_thresh. (1 day)

Notes to self / heuristics to try in sim code:
- Use exponential moving average for observed util to drive price, not instantaneous rps (smoother).
- Add hysteresis to route switching to avoid ping-pong (route stickiness).
- Model limited visibility: router uses shard-local util estimate which can diverge; check effect of noisy signals.
- Log tail event triggers: if >k tenants see p95>threshold for t consecutive windows, mark as systemic.

Tiny ascii diagram of flow (conceptual):

Tenant request -> Router (observed util + price table) -> route choice -> route queue -> backend (latency distribution)
                     |                              ^
                     +-- price update loop (EWA of util) -+

Tasks (short):
- [ ] spin up notebook skeleton (sim.py) + parameter json schema
- [ ] implement route price function + util EWA
- [ ] baseline scenario (beta=0.3, gamma=1.0) + plot latency/cost
- [ ] add tenant QoS budget accounting
- [ ] prepare short experiment doc + slides for infra sync

Quick hypotheses to test in first run (if true, note implications):
- H1: modest beta (0.5) reduces long tail frequency by shifting mid-value traffic earlier -> implies we can tune beta as a lightweight congestion control without heavy controls.
- H2: too aggressive beta (>=1.5) increases overall spend due to migration to dedicated for many tenants -> implies need per-tenant caps or progressive beta by tenant tier.
- H3: adding small burst credits reduces perceived p95 incidents significantly with minimal cost (fast wins).

References / scratch links:
- routing price signals convo in #runtime-pricing (slack ts 2025-10-19)
- GH: redwood/runtime#4821 (early router price signal prototype)
- Confluence draft: ingress-price-signals (linked above)

Questions for reviewers:
- Do we prefer a price-driven router or quota-first? (quota-first: enforce strict token budgets then route fallback; price-driven: economic nudging)
- How much operational explainability do we need? (we should be able to explain per-tenant why a request hit X route)
- Any hard constraints from sales/finance on per-request minimum cost assumptions?

Longer-term ideas (brainstorm):
- Use ML model to predict per-tenant short-term demand and pre-adjust price curves per shard to reduce oscillation.
- Expose a tenant-facing simulator UI (simple sliders for QoS budget / sensitivity) so customers can preview cost/latency tradeoffs.
- Tie quality monitoring: if fallback variants increase error/degeneration, automatically reduce beta (protect quality).

End of scratchpad. This will be cleaned into a proper experiment doc once sim runs produce clear plots.
